The fog did not roll in at Blackwood Point; it descended like a heavy, wet wool blanket, suffocating the world until there was only the sound of the surf and the rhythmic, mechanical heartbeat of the light.

Elias Thorne was not the keeper of Blackwood Point. He was the Keeper of the Void. Or, as the official, redacted logs of the Maritime Authority listed him, *Subject Zero*.

He had no number on his uniform. He had no name in the registry. He had only the key to the lantern room and a silence so profound it felt like a physical weight.

### The Descent

The supply boat, the *Aethelgard*, docked every forty days. It brought kerosene, canned peaches, fresh linen, and a new journal. It also brought silence from the outside world. The captain, a grizzled man named Halloway who looked at Elias with a mixture of pity and fear, never stayed past sunset. He never asked questions. He never looked Elias in the eye for too long.

"Keep the wick trimmed, Zero," Halloway would mutter, tossing the crate onto the wet stone pier. "And don’t look at the water after midnight. Not ever."

Then the engine would cough, sputter, and fade into the gray mist, leaving Elias alone on the jagged tooth of rock that jutted out from the sea like a broken finger.

The sea does not forgive, and it rarely forgets. But the Lighthouse of the Void, perched on the jagged spine of Rock Zero, remembered nothing at all. It was a structure of black basalt and rusted iron, standing alone in the churning grey expanse of the Atlantic, far beyond any shipping lane, far beyond any map.

There was no official designation for the keeper of Rock Zero. The logs of the Coast Guard, if they even knew the rock existed, listed it as "Uninhabited Hazard." But every full moon, a small, rusted skiff would arrive, bearing a man who called himself Lighthouse Keeper #0.

His name was Elias Thorne, though he had not spoken it aloud in twenty years. He was a man carved from the same granite as the tower—weathered, grey, and immovable. He wore a uniform that had long ago lost its color, patched with fabrics from eras he could barely recall. His eyes were the color of storm clouds, perpetually looking outward, never inward.

The lighthouse itself was an anomaly. It did not emit a beam of light that cut through the fog. Instead, it emitted a *shadow*. A cone of absolute darkness that spiraled upward into the night sky, a void in the fabric of the world. Sailors who passed too close reported a sudden drop in temperature, a feeling of being watched by something ancient, and a profound sense of peace that bordered on coma. Some called it a curse. Others called it a mercy. Elias knew it as a duty.
